title: Frontend CI/CD Automation
content:
5.8.4. Set up CI/CD flow for Frontend with AWS CodePipeline Instead of manually running a build command and dragging and dropping files to S3 every time you update the interface, we will have AWS do this completely automatically whenever there is new code pushed to GitHub.
Prerequisites: You have pushed the Frontend source code folder to a repository on GitHub and the root directory contains the buildspec.yml configuration file for the frontend.
Step 1: Initialize CodePipeline
Search for and access the CodePipeline service on the AWS Console. Click Create pipeline. Pipeline name: Enter a name, e.g., smart-campus-frontend-pipeline. Service role: Select New service role (so AWS automatically creates permissions for the Pipeline). Click Next. Step 2: Configure Source (Code source)
Source provider: Select GitHub (via GitHub App). Click the Connect to GitHub button. Enter a connection name (e.g., github-smart-campus) and follow the on-screen instructions to Authorize AWS to access your GitHub account. Select the Repository containing your Frontend code and click Install & Authorize. Then click Connect. Return to the Source configuration page, ensure the Repository, Branch (e.g., main), and CodePipeline default are selected. Click Next. Step 3: Configure Build (Compiler)
Build provider: Select AWS CodeBuild. Choose Region ap-southeast-1. Click the Create project button, a new window will appear. Name the project (e.g., smart-campus-frontend-build). Environment: Select the Amazon Linux operating system, Runtime Standard, the latest Image version (aws/codebuild/amazonlinux2-x86_64-standard...). Scroll down to the Buildspec section, select Use a buildspec file (pointing to the frontend’s buildspec-frontend.yml file). Scroll down to the bottom and click Continue to CodePipeline. Return to the CodePipeline window, click Next. Step 4: Configure Deploy (Deployment)
Deploy provider: Select Amazon S3. Region: Same as the S3 Bucket’s Region. Bucket: Select the static S3 Bucket name you created in lesson 5.8.2 (e.g., smart-campus-frontend-2026). Check the Extract file before deploy box (Very important, to unpack the ZIP file containing the build code). Click Next, review the configuration, and then click Create pipeline. Step 5: Practical Experience Every time you change the interface, edit text, change colors, then commit and git push to the main branch. You go back to CodePipeline and will see the Pipeline automatically run from Source -> Build -> Deploy. When complete, reload the webpage and the new interface is live!

title: Monitoring Testing
content:
5.10.4. Log, Metric, and Tracing Testing (CloudWatch & X-Ray) This section guides you to view real-time logs, check metrics, and analyze request flows via X-Ray to confirm the monitoring system is operating correctly.
Step 1: View Lambda Logs on CloudWatch
Go to AWS Console > CloudWatch > Log groups. Find and select the log group named /aws/lambda/smart-campus-api. From the Log streams list, click on the newest stream (usually the top row with the most recent timestamp). You will see detailed event log lines for each API call, including: Request start and end times Result returned from Rekognition Record info written to DynamoDB Event emitted to EventBridge Expected Result: Logs clearly show processing steps, with no ERROR or Exception lines.
Step 2: Check Lambda Metrics
Go to CloudWatch, look at the left menu under Metrics > Select Classic metrics. At the Browse tab below the chart, select the AWS/Lambda namespace. Continue selecting the By Function Name dimension. Find the smart-campus-api function and check the metrics to track: Invocations: Number of function calls (should increase corresponding to the number of times you tested) Duration: Average processing time (ms) Errors: Number of errors (expected to be 0) Adjust the time range on the toolbar (e.g., 1h or 3h) and observe the chart. Expected Result: The chart displays API activity data, not empty.

title: Event-Driven Architecture
content:
Part 4: Event-Driven Architecture Up to this point, our attendance API operates on a Synchronous mechanism. This means that when a user uploads an image, the API Gateway sends it to Lambda. Lambda calls AI, saves to DB, saves to S3, and only then returns a successful result to the Frontend.
This approach has a drawback: If we want to add features like “Send a successful attendance Email” or “Security alert if a stranger is detected”, stuffing all the code into the initial Lambda function will drastically increase the Response Time, leading to poor user experience (long wait times) or even Timeouts.
To solve this problem, we will apply the Event-Driven Architecture with AWS’s classic trio of tools:
Amazon EventBridge: A transit hub (Event Bus) that receives and routes events. Amazon SNS (Simple Notification Service): A Pub/Sub system used to broadcast notifications to multiple endpoints (like Email, SMS, etc.). Amazon SQS (Simple Queue Service): A queue that temporarily stores messages for asynchronous processing, preventing system overload. Amazon SES (Simple Email Service): A dedicated email sending service. New Processing Flow: After saving to the DB, instead of independently sending an Email, the main Lambda function (in section 5.5) does only one thing: Emits an Event containing CHECKIN_SUCCESS (Attendance successful) or SECURITY_ALERT (Security alert) to EventBridge. Immediately after emitting the Event, Lambda responds with the result to the user (very fast!). In the background, EventBridge will use Rules to catch these Events and route them: SECURITY_ALERT events will be pushed straight to an SNS Topic to instantly send security alerts. CHECKIN_SUCCESS events will be pushed into an SQS Queue acting as a buffer, then another Worker (or direct processing) will pull the info, combine it with Amazon SES to send attendance report Emails to HR. title: Data Analytics (S3 & Athena)
content:
Goal In the previous sections, whenever a user checkin, the system saves the result into DynamoDB (for fast per-user querying) and emits an event via EventBridge to SQS/SNS. Simultaneously, we also have an Analytics Worker Lambda function (responding to the SQS queue) that automatically pulls these attendance events and writes directly as JSON files into an S3 Data Lake.
Once the data safely resides in the Data Lake, we can use AWS Glue to automatically infer the table schema, and use Amazon Athena to query the data using SQL. This entire process is fully automated, serverless, and isolated from the main API system (OLTP). Instead of having to query DynamoDB (which is very expensive and unsuitable for large statistical queries), we will use a Serverless Data Lake architecture with AWS Glue and Amazon Athena.
AWS Glue (Crawler): Automatically scans Log files in the S3 Data Lake to identify the data structure (Schema) and create a virtual table. Amazon Athena: Allows you to write familiar SQL statements to query data residing in S3 directly through the virtual Glue table, without needing to install any Database Server. You pay per amount of data scanned (Pay per query). Detailed Practice Content Please click on each item below in the left menu bar or click directly on the links below to follow the detailed steps:

Goal To ensure the Smart Campus system always operates stably and is ready to respond when an incident occurs, we need tools to monitor the health of the system, view error logs, and measure performance.
Amazon CloudWatch: Acts as a monitoring hub. It will collect Logs (activity journals) from Lambda, API Gateway, and EventBridge. It also provides Metrics (indicators) and Alarms (alerts) when there are abnormalities (e.g., a sudden increase in the number of errors). AWS X-Ray: An extremely powerful Trace tool for Serverless architectures. X-Ray will draw a visual connection map between services (Client -> API Gateway -> Lambda -> DynamoDB) and point out exactly where the bottleneck is, how many milliseconds it takes at each stage. title: Resource Cleanup
content:
5.11. Resource Cleanup (Clean-up) After completing the Workshop, please delete all created resources to avoid incurring unwanted costs on your AWS account.
Below is the list of resources to delete in a safe order (delete dependent resources first):
Step 1: Delete CloudFront Distributions
Go to CloudFront > Distributions. Select the smart-campus-frontend distribution (from lesson 5.8.3): Click Disable and wait for the status to change to Disabled. Then click Delete. Do the same with the smart-campus-api-cf distribution (from lesson 5.5.4). Step 2: Delete CodePipeline and CodeBuild
Go to CodePipeline > Select smart-campus-backend-pipeline > Click Delete pipeline. Next, delete smart-campus-frontend-pipeline. Go to CodeBuild > Delete the projects smart-campus-backend-build and smart-campus-frontend-build. Step 3: Delete API Gateway
Go to API Gateway > Select the SmartCampusHTTPApi API > Click Delete. Step 4: Delete Lambda Functions
Go to Lambda > Functions. Delete one by one: smart-campus-api smart-campus-analytics-worker Step 5: Delete EventBridge Rules
Go to Amazon EventBridge > Rules. Delete attendance-recorded-to-sns and attendance-to-sqs. Step 6: Delete SQS Queues
Go to SQS > Delete smart-campus-analytics-queue. Next, delete smart-campus-dlq. Step 7: Delete SNS Topics
Go to SNS > Topics > Delete smart-campus-notifications. Go to Subscriptions > Delete related Subscriptions. Step 8: Delete CloudWatch Alarms and Log Groups
Go to CloudWatch > Alarms > Delete the alarm Lambda-Error-Alert. Go to Log groups > Delete /aws/lambda/smart-campus-api and /aws/lambda/smart-campus-analytics-worker. Go to WAF Logs > Delete log group aws-waf-logs-smartcampus. Step 9: Delete WAF Web ACL
Go to WAF & Shield > Web ACLs (select Global/CloudFront scope). Delete SmartCampusAPIWebACL. Go to IP sets > Delete SmartCampusIPSet. Step 10: Delete DynamoDB Tables
Go to DynamoDB > Tables. Delete all tables one by one: smart-campus-attendance, smart-campus-faces, smart-campus-users, smart-campus-security, smart-campus-notifications, smart-campus-settings, smart-campus-tasks, smart-campus-leaves, smart-campus-holidays. Step 11: Delete S3 Buckets
[!WARNING] You must delete all objects inside before you can delete a bucket.
Go to S3, for each following bucket: smart-campus-images-{id} smart-campus-frontend-2026 smart-campus-datalake-{id} Bucket saving Athena results Go inside the bucket > Select all objects > Delete. Then exit and delete the bucket. Step 12: Delete Rekognition Collection
Open AWS CloudShell and run the command:
aws rekognition delete-collection --collection-id smart-campus-faces --region ap-southeast-1 Step 13: Delete Cognito User Pool
Go to Amazon Cognito > User Pools. Select the User Pool you created > Click Delete. Step 14: Delete IAM Roles
Go to IAM > Roles. Delete the roles: smart-campus-api-role-..., smart-campus-analytics-worker-role-..., AWSGlueServiceRole-SmartCampus, and roles automatically created by CodeBuild/CodePipeline. Step 15: Delete Glue Crawler and Database
Go to AWS Glue > Crawlers > Delete smart-campus-attendance-crawler. Go to Databases > Delete smart_campus_db. Step 16: Delete SES Identities
Go to Amazon SES > Verified identities. Select your verified email address > Click Delete. ✅ Check Completion After finishing deletion, go to AWS Cost Explorer or Billing Dashboard to confirm that no resources are running and incurring costs. Congratulations on completing the entire Smart Campus Platform on AWS Workshop! 🎉
